intro: The Daodejing is about five thousand Chinese characters long. It is one of the most translated books in the world. Its lines are short, strange and open. A single line about water or an empty bowl can mean something to a poet, a ruler, a potter and a Daoist priest.

In this unit you read key chapters slowly, in James Legge's 1891 translation. You start with naming, opposites, water and emptiness in chapters 1, 2, 8, 11 and 16. Then you turn to the chapters about rulers and states: 17, 57, 60, 67 and 80. You meet readers from Han Feizi to Tang emperors to modern writers.

By the end you will be able to cite the Daodejing by chapter, explain terms such as Dao, de, wu wei, ziran and paradox, compare Legge with a paraphrase, and describe how political, personal and religious readers take the same lines.
bigQuestion: How can a short book that doubts words be read in so many ways, and what does a careful reader do with that?

timeline.t: Traditional time of Laozi, said to be an older contemporary of Confucius
Many scholars think the text is taking shape (dates debated)
Guodian bamboo slips copy parts of the text
Death of Han Feizi, who wrote chapters explaining the Laozi
Mawangdui silk copies are made, De part first
Sima Qian writes Laozi's biography in the Shiji
Tang Emperor Xuanzong writes a commentary
Legge's Tao Teh King appears in Sacred Books of the East 39
The Mawangdui silk texts are excavated
The Guodian bamboo slips are excavated

words.d: "the way"; the source and pattern of all things; Legge spells it Tao
virtue or power; the second word in the title Daodejing
paired forces that shape and balance each other
a statement that seems contradictory but may point to a truth
what is not there; the empty space that makes things useful
the wise person or ruler who follows the Dao
gentleness or compassion, economy, and not putting oneself first (ch. 67)
a text written by hand, such as on bamboo or silk
an early school stressing strict laws, rewards and punishments
a restatement of a passage in different words

test.q: Which chapter opens with the Tao that can be trodden?
Which image does chapter 8 use for the highest excellence?
test.why: Chapter 8 says the highest excellence is like water.

test.q: In chapter 11, what makes a wheel useful?
choices: The empty space at its hub
test.why: The use of the wheel depends on the empty space.

test.q: What does chapter 2 say about opposites?
choices: They give rise to each other
test.why: Chapter 2 lists pairs that arise together.

test.q: Which chapter ranks rulers from barely known to despised?
What does chapter 60 compare governing to?
test.why: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.

test.q: Which chapter describes a small state within earshot of its neighbors?
Which Legalist read the Laozi as advice for a strong ruler?
test.why: Han Feizi wrote chapters explaining the Laozi.

test.q: What did the Mawangdui silk copies show?
choices: The De part placed before the Dao part
test.why: The 1973 finds put the De part first.

test.q: Why does Legge spell the word Tao?
choices: It is a different word from Dao
test.why: Tao is Wade-Giles; Dao is pinyin.

test.q: How do religious Daoists honor Laozi?
choices: As Taishang Laojun, a divine being
test.why: Religious Daoism honors Laozi as the Most High Lord Lao.

test.q: What does chapter 16 call returning to the root?
test.why: Returning to the root is called stillness.

test.q: How do the Analects and Daodejing differ on ritual?
choices: The Analects values li; the Daodejing is often wary of it
The Daodejing values li; the Analects rejects it
test.why: Analects 2.3 praises li; Daodejing 38 calls ritual a thin form of loyalty.
A paraphrase restates a passage in new words.

test.q: What does Heshang Gong's commentary often read "the state" as?
test.why: Heshang Gong reads governing the state and caring for the body together.

write.prompt: Is the Daodejing a book about ruling a state or about living a life? Cite two or three chapters (for example ch. 8, 17 and 60 in Legge's 1891 translation), explain what each says, and describe how at least two kinds of readers have taken them.
tips: Cite by chapter and name Legge's 1891 translation or say you paraphrase.
Attribute every reading: "Han Feizi read," "religious Daoists read," "some scholars argue."
Use the unit's terms, such as wu wei, ziran and sage, with a short gloss.
Compare readings rather than judging which is true.
